nameStory: This ivy gets its name from its native home in the Canary Islands, that chain of volcanic islands off the coast of Africa. Spanish explorers named those islands after the wild dogs ("canis" in Latin) they found there, so this plant carries the legacy of those ancient canine inhabitants in its scientific name.
description: Canary Islands Ivy is a climbing evergreen vine that can scramble up trees, walls, and fences using tiny rootlets along its stems. It has glossy, dark green leaves that are larger and more leathery than our common English ivy. This vigorous climber can reach impressive heights when it finds good support, creating dense curtains of foliage that stay green year-round. Though native to the Canary Islands, it's occasionally grown as an ornamental in New England gardens.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Large, glossy dark green leaves that feel thick and leathery to the touch, typically 4-6 inches across with 3-5 broad lobes that are less deeply cut than common ivy

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Vigorous climbing vine that uses small aerial rootlets along the stems to grip surfaces, creating dense evergreen coverage

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Thick, sturdy stems that feel substantial compared to common ivy, often with a reddish tinge when young

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small, greenish-yellow flowers in globe-shaped clusters appear on mature plants in fall, followed by dark blue-black berries

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: Leaves have a distinctive waxy, almost plastic-like feel that's noticeably thicker and more substantial than other ivy species

habitat: In New England, Canary Islands Ivy is extremely rare in the wild, with only 2 recorded observations. When found, it's typically as an escape from cultivation near homes or gardens where it was planted as an ornamental. It prefers sheltered locations with some protection from harsh winter winds.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges as bright green shoots, and the evergreen leaves provide easy identification as they contrast with awakening native vegetation.
seasonality.summer: Mature foliage is at its glossiest, making the thick, leathery leaf texture most apparent for identification.
seasonality.fall: Mature plants may produce small clusters of greenish-yellow flowers, though flowering plants are rare in New England's climate.
seasonality.winter: Evergreen leaves remain glossy and identifiable, though they may show some browning or damage from cold temperatures in exposed locations.

funFact: Despite being called an "ivy," this plant can actually develop into a small tree-like form when it reaches maturity and stops climbing, completely changing its leaf shape and growth pattern in a Jekyll-and-Hyde transformation that few people ever witness.
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with common English ivy, but Canary Islands Ivy has noticeably larger, thicker, more leathery leaves with broader, less pointed lobes. Memory trick: "Canary Islands Ivy has leaves as large and substantial as the islands themselves are compared to tiny Britain."
contextualKnowledge: This species is sometimes called "Madeira Ivy" in the horticultural trade, which can cause confusion since Madeira is a different Atlantic island group. In New England, it's much less cold-hardy than common ivy, which explains why it's so rarely encountered in the wild here.
compareHints: Canary Islands Ivy stands out from its relatives by its distinctly larger, thicker leaves and more robust stems. Common ivy has smaller, thinner leaves with more pointed lobes, while Atlantic ivy falls somewhere in between. Persian ivy also has large leaves but tends to be even less cold-tolerant in New England conditions.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Common ivy is by far the most widespread Hedera species in New England.
Atlantic ivy differs from common ivy by having larger, thicker leaves and more vigorous growth.
Persian ivy stands out from its ivy relatives primarily by size - it has the largest leaves and most vigorous growth of any Hedera species.
